cemetery_profile.name: South-View Cemetery
distinction: Oldest African American cemetery in Atlanta
Oldest African American non-eleemosynary (non-charitable) stockholder corporation in the United States
Founded by nine formerly enslaved African American businessmen
Listed on Georgia Register of Historic Places (2026)
Pending National Register of Historic Places listing — NPS reference BC100013186
cemetery_profile.founding_story: South-View Cemetery was founded in response to the indignities African Americans faced at Atlanta's segregated burial grounds. Oakland Cemetery (est. 1850) maintained a 'Slave Square,' and in 1877 the Atlanta City Council ordered the exhumation and mass reinterment of its 860+ occupants to resell the land to white buyers. Westview Cemetery (est. 1884) confined African Americans to a segregated section called 'Rest Haven,' accessible only through a back gate. Albert Watts watched his father Sterling Watts buried through that back gate in October 1885. Six months later, on April 26, 1886, Watts and five other formerly enslaved men chartered South-View Cemetery Association — a burial ground owned and controlled entirely by African Americans.

historical_context.topic: Racial Segregation in Atlanta Cemeteries — Why South-View Was Founded
historical_context.content: Until the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s, Atlanta's cemeteries were segregated by law and tradition. Oakland Cemetery (est. 1850) designated 'Slave Square' in 1852 — a section for both free and enslaved African Americans. By the Civil War's end, 860+ people were buried there. In 1877, the Atlanta City Council voted to exhume Slave Square, rebury the remains in the colored pauper grounds (many anonymously in a mass grave), and resell the lots. The exact location of their reburial remains unknown. Westview Cemetery (est. 1884) maintained 'Rest Haven,' a segregated section for African Americans accessible only through a back gate several hundred yards past the main entrance. These indignities — combined with African American petitions to the city council in early 1878 for either additional burial space or a separate cemetery — directly motivated the founding of South-View in 1886.

historical_context.topic: Founding and Early History of South-View Cemetery
historical_context.content: South-View Cemetery Association was chartered April 26, 1886 — six months after Albert Watts watched his father buried through Westview's back gate. The first organizational meeting was held at Friendship Baptist Church. Early investors included fraternal orders (Grand United Order of Odd Fellows) and church benevolent societies (Daughters of Bethel). South-View claims the distinction of being the oldest African American stockholder corporation in the United States. The cemetery was originally 25 acres; by 1946 it had expanded to approximately 90 acres; it now covers over 100 acres. In 1961, the cemetery dedicated a monument to its founders and early board members, listing charter members and 16 deceased board members including Alonzo F. Herndon, David T. Howard, and Charles S. Cox. Mary L. Bentley, office manager for 48 years, is the sole woman named on the memorial as of 2017.

historical_context.topic: Categories of Notable Residents at South-View
historical_context.content: South-View's historic section reflects the full breadth of African American life in Atlanta. Notable 19th-century burials include Alonzo F. Herndon (Atlanta Life Insurance founder, Atlanta's first Black millionaire); Bishop Henry McNeal Turner (AME leader, Reconstruction legislator); George Wilder and Frank Smith (killed in the 1906 Atlanta Race Riot). 20th-century notables include Moses Amos (Georgia's first licensed Black pharmacist); Alice Dugged Cary (first Auburn Avenue Library librarian); 1st Lt. Walter Westmoreland (Tuskegee Airman); John Wesley Dobbs ('Mayor of Sweet Auburn'); Grace Towns Hamilton (first Black woman in Georgia legislature); Julian Bond (scholar, civil rights activist); Hank Aaron (baseball legend); Herman J. Russell (entrepreneur). Atlanta Child Murder victims buried at South-View: Milton Harvey, Yusef Bell, Aaron Wyche, Aaron Jackson, Patrick Rogers, Curtis Walker, William Barrett. 21st-century notables include Jesse Hill Jr. (first Black chair, Georgia Board of Regents); Asa Yancey (first Black faculty at Emory Medical School); Mattiwilda Dobbs (first Black at La Scala opera). Originally buried here but moved: Martin Luther King Jr. (1968, now at MLK Center), Lt. Henry Ossian Flipper (1940, reinterred Thomasville, GA), Dr. Benjamin E. Mays (1984, moved to Morehouse memorial).

historical_context.topic: South-View Cemetery and the Civil Rights Movement
historical_context.content: South-View is inseparable from Atlanta's Civil Rights history. Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King (MLK Jr.'s parents) are interred in a marble crypt at South-View. All deceased pastors of historic Ebenezer Baptist Church (as of 2016) are buried here. Fred C. Bennette (d. 1994) was one of MLK Jr.'s closest aides; his epitaph was written by Andrew Young. Theodore Martin Alexander provided Lloyd's of London liability insurance for cars used in the Montgomery Bus Boycott. Grace Towns Hamilton was the first Black woman elected to any Deep South state legislature (Georgia, 1965). Jesse Hill Jr. was the first Black member and chair of the Georgia Board of Regents. Julian Bond (1940-2015) — scholar, SNCC co-founder, NAACP chair — is buried here. MLK Jr. himself was temporarily buried at South-View in 1968 before being moved to the King Center.

historical_context.topic: Atlanta Child Murder Victims Buried at South-View
historical_context.content: From 1979 to 1981, approximately 29 African American children, teenagers, and young adults were kidnapped and murdered in Atlanta in what became known as the Atlanta Child Murders. Several victims' families chose South-View Cemetery as their sons' final resting place. Victims buried at South-View include: Milton Harvey, Yusef Bell, Aaron Wyche, Aaron Jackson, Patrick Rogers, Curtis Walker, and William Barrett.

historical_context.topic: Funerary Art, Symbolism, and Memorial Traditions at South-View
historical_context.content: South-View's landscape reflects 19th-century garden cemetery aesthetics combined with African American vernacular traditions. Victorian funerary symbols throughout the historic section include obelisks, urns, and angels. Fraternal and benevolent order symbols — Odd Fellows, Masons, Good Samaritans — appear on many markers. Children's gravestones often feature lambs, flowers, and cradle imagery. Vernacular African American traditions include concrete aggregate markers (manufactured locally by Eldren Bailey), seashells, and personal items placed on graves. Cedar and yucca plants are traditional plantings. Adinkra symbols from West African (Akan/Ghana) tradition are referenced in the book's illustrations. Epitaphs range from biblical verse to fraternal mottos to personal tributes — Fred Bennette's gravestone bears the motto 'Commandante' with an epitaph written by Andrew Young.

historical_context.topic: African American Funeral Industry Connected to South-View
historical_context.content: South-View was central to Atlanta's African American funeral industry during segregation. David T. Howard (undertaker) was an original South-View board member and investor. Cox Brothers Funeral Home (est. 1900) was founded by Charles S. Cox; his widow Addie managed it. Geneva Moton Haugabrooks opened Haugabrooks Funeral Home on Auburn Avenue in 1929. Henry M. Ivey was an undertaker listed on the South-View memorial. Eldren Matthew Bailey (d. 1987) ran a small business manufacturing distinctive concrete grave markers for Atlanta's African American funeral homes — these markers are a vernacular art form documented throughout South-View's historic section. Appendix B of the source book lists early African American undertakers and funeral homes in Atlanta.

historical_context.topic: African American Fraternal and Benevolent Organizations at South-View
historical_context.content: During segregation, African American fraternal and benevolent organizations provided social insurance, community support, and political organizing. Many organizations purchased group burial lots at South-View. Organizations represented include: Grand United Order of Odd Fellows; Prince Hall Masons; Daughters of Bethel; Good Samaritans; Grand Chief of the State Grand Lodge of Good Samaritans; and various church benevolent societies affiliated with AME, Baptist, Methodist, and Congregational churches. The Leonard Street Orphans Home has a burial lot in South-View's historic section. Appendix A of the source book lists early African American benevolent organizations in Atlanta.

people.biography: Pharmacist. Following in the footsteps of his uncle Moses Amos, Georgia's first African American licensed pharmacist, Miles Amos be- came proprietor of the West Side Drug Store upon his uncle's death in 1928. The next year the store began advertising as Amos' Drugstore. Amos worked his way through Wilberforce College in Ohio with a summer job as a Pullman Porter. He graduated from Cincinnati College of Pharmacy in 1928. In 1953, Amos and two other African Americans, Austin Thomas Walden and Roderick Badger Harris, won a court deci- sion to qualify for election to the City Executive Committee, a nonpartisan political organization responsible for conducting Atlanta's primary elections. Amos won over Harris, and Walden ran unopposed. Amos continued to be involved with Atlanta's civic and political affairs throughout his life, and he was a lifetime member of the NAACP.He married his cousin India DeLaine Amos

Though the Grady Memorial Hospital School of Nursing opened in 1898, African Americans were not offered training until 1914 when Andrews organized the Grady Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses. She served as superintendent of the school until 1922. Beginning in 1922, Grady's white American nursing officials began directing the school; in 1965, the two schools were combined. The National Conclave of Grady Graduate Nurses preserves the history of the African American nursing school and Andrew's legacy as its founder. Andrews was superintendent of the MacVicar Hospital at Spelman College from 1928 to 1948. She graduated from MacVicar's nurse training program in 1906 and that same year was hired as superintendent of Atlanta's Lula Grove Training School for Colored Nurses. Andrews was involved in many health and community service organizations-she was an original board member of the Atlanta Urban League, vol- unteered with the Community Chest, served as a board member in the colored branch of the Atlanta Tuberculosis Association, and was a life member of the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA She was a charter member of the Neighborhood Union and served as its second president from 1937 to 1942. A community center for African Americans in Gainesville, Georgia, was named in her honor. Archer, Samuel Howard

DICTIONARY 171 school, purchasing agent, dean. and acting president Archer played football at Im alma mater, Colgate University in New York, and he coached the football team at Morehouse from 1905 to 1908 and from 1912 to 1915, winning a total of five confer- ence championships. He married a classmate, Anna Courbley Johnson (d. 1946 ), whom he met at Wayland Academyin Washington, D. C. The two competed academ- ically for highest honors, and she often insisted that she came in second only because of male preference. people.biography: Barbershop Owner, Domestic Servant. Austin was ten years old when slavery ended. His education included only a few years at a small church school, Perry Chapel, in Franklin County, Georgia. With his partner, W. A Stovall, Austin opened the first barbershop owned by African Americans on Auburn Avenue. He later moved the barbershop to Houston and Butler, and in 1927, he sold the busin~. In their later years, Austin and his wife Adline ( d. 1938) began working as butler and cook for the C. T. Latsons, a white American family. As Mrs. Latson lay dying. she asked Adline to continue taking care of the younger Latson daughter, Le- ola. When Leola was to be engaged, her suitor asked Adline's approval. Adline agreed, with the condition that the young man treat Leola well, "If you can't be good to her, why just bring her right back to me." Upon C. T. Latson's death, Adline re- ceived a bequest, the same amount given to his children. After Austen's retirement, at Leola's request, Austen began receiving a monthly pension from the Latson family. Austen died at age ninety-five. He outlived Adline and all their eleven children. 172 LJ-.(;A(Y 11.Jl)J-:A'I II B Bailey, Eldren Matthew

people.biography: Minister, Civil Rights Leader. Bearden was pas- tor of Big Bethel AME Church in the 1950s and 6os. He was a graduate of Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary. An outspoken civil rights leader, he used his weekly radio broadcasts from Big Bethel to preach against segregation. He was active in community development and served as president of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP. Bearden was elected the eighty-third bishop of the AME Church in 1964. He served as chair of the board of trustees of Morris Brown and was instrumental in helping the school achieve accreditation. Bellamy, Walter Jones

people.biography: Basketball Player. A native of New Bern, North Carolina, and a graduate of Indiana University, Bellamy was a member of the 1960 U.S. Olympic gold medal basketball team. He started his professional career with the Chicago Packers, and in 1962, he was named National Basketball Association (NBA) Rookie of the Year. He became a leading scorer and rebounder during his fourteen-season career in the NBA by amassing 20,941 points, an average of 20.1 points per game, and fielding 14,241 rebounds, an average of 13.7 rebounds per game. He was a four-time NBA All-Star player. Bellamy was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1993. In retirement, Bellamy was active with the NAACP,the Atlanta Urban League, and the YMCA.He also served on the board of directors of the Historic South-View Preservation Foundation. Bennette, Fred C. Jr.

people.biography: Minister, Civil Rights Leader. Bennette was a graduate of Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary. He played a crucial role in the leadership and organization of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC).While still a student at Morris Brown, he led the sit-in campaign to desegregate Rich's depart1nent store in Atlanta. He directed SCLC voter registra- tion drives, and he was deputy director of the Georgia Voters League. He was the first director of the SCLC'sOperation Bread Basket, a community project which engaged African American churches to challenge employment practices with the goal of desegregating workplaces. Bennett was one of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s closest and most trusted aids, and he served as advisor to Georgia Governor Jimmy Carter and to U. S. Ambassador Andrew Young when Young was mayor of Atlanta. Bennette was a member of the board of advisors and security director for The Martin Luther King Jr. Center for Non-Violent Social Change. Bennette's gravestone bears the motto "Commandante." Andrew Young wrote Bennette's epitaph: "You were always there when Martin needed you-ready to lay down your life for a friend. God has blessed you. Peace." Benning, Eula

people.biography: Nurse. Benning was a graduate of the Grady School of Nursing, and she earned a bachelor of science in nursing education from New York University. She served as supervisor of public health nurses for Atlanta and Fulton County and was an executive committee member of the National Nursing Associa- tion. Benning was an advocate for the education and professional recognition of African American nurses, and she founded the Atlanta School for Practical Nurse Education in 1963. Benning was the last president of the Georgia State Nurses Association, an African American organization which she helped integrate into the state organi1.ation for white American nurses. A group of practical nurses who grad- uated only two weeks prior from Benning's school were among the professional nurses who served as flower ladies at her funeral. The Atlanta Chapter of the Grady Nurses Conclave, the Eula Benning Club, was named in her honor. She married Clinton Benning

people.biography: Accountant, Banker, Educator. Blayton, a WWI vet- eran, was a founder and secretary of the Pioneer Store Company in Oklahoma. In Atlanta, he was an auditor at Standard Life Insurance Company. He became the first African American certified public accountant (CPA) in Georgia in 1928. He opened an accounting firm, and he taught accounting and economics at Morehouse College, Atlanta University, and Morris Brown College. Blayton was a co-founder of the Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Association, a significant financier of African Americanhome loans, and he served as cashier and vice president for Citizens Trust Bank. In 1949, Blayton purchased WERD, the first radio station in the U. S. to be owned by African Americans. He was inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 1995. Slayton married Willa Mae Daniels

WWII ended, and Bohannon became an officer-pilot in the all African American 332 nd Fighter Group stationed at Godman Field in Ken- tucky. After leavingthe military, Bohannon headed the Southern Regional Commission's Georgia Veterans Service Project for African American servicemen. He also worked for the U. S. Post Office.He returned to Lincoln University where he had begun his studies years before and earned his degree in 1948. Bohannon worked for fifteen years in the Fulton County School System before becoming the first African American to hold the position of regional Management Training Officer with the U.S. Post Office.Bohannon later worked in the regional office of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare. At the 1968 Demo- oatic National Convention in Chicago, Illinois, he was spontaneously nominated as a vice presidential candidate, however, he was too young to hold office. Bond co- founded the Southern Poverty Law Center and served as its president He was pres- ident of the Atlanta branch of the NAACPbefore becoming chairrnan of the National NAACP.Bond was also a television commentator, newspaper columnist, poet, and college profeswr. people.biography: Chief of the Eastern Cherokee. Bushyhead was an American Indian chief from North Carolina who fought for the Confederate Army during the CivilWar. At some point during his time in the military, he was reportedly promoted to Colonel and thus was called by that title after the war ended. In 1869, Bushyheadwas elected council chairman which gave him the authority to represent the eastern Cherokees in Washington, D. C. Each Spring, Bushyhead traveled to Atlanta to solicit funds for his tribe. In May 1892, during his annual trip, he became gravelyill. He died in the African American boarding house where he had been stay- ing and was buried at South-View by undertaker Mitchell Cargile. The news of Bushyhead'sburial in an African American cemetery prompted local white Ameri- cans to suggest that funds be raised to move his body to the Confederate section of Oakland, the city cemetery. Whether Bushyhead was ever moved to Oakland, or returned to North Carolina, remains unknown. 184 l.EGACY(N DEATH C Calhoun, John Henry Jr.

people.biography: Carpenter, Building Contractor. According to Atlanta historian Edward R. Carter, Hamilton served in the Union Army during the CivilWar, was elected to the city council of Eufaula, Alabama, and served two terms in Alabama's Reconstruction Legislature. Hamilton built many fine homes in Eufala, including his own. He was given a gold watch and a piece of property by the city of Eufala for the part he played in preventing a fire and robbery secretly being plotted by African Americans. By 1876, Hamilton had moved his family to Atlanta and started the construction company of Alexander Hamilton and Son. Hamilton's obituary in the Atlanta Constitution on May 27, 1911, noted that "some of the best-known buildings in Atlanta were erected by him." Two of those structures included the Good Samaritan building on Ivy Street and the Linton Hopkins House in Ansley Park. Hamilton also built many of the large houses on Peachtree and Washington streets. He worked as superintendent at W. L. Trainer & Company for several years, and he also was the contractor for Morris Brown College. Hamilton was one of the organizers of the Georgia Real Estate Loan and Trust Company and a member of the National Negro Business League. people.biography: Educator, Politician, Activist. Hamilton was the first African-American woman in the deep South to be elected as a state legisla- tor. An Atlanta native, Hamilton graduated from Atlanta University and earned a master's degree from Ohio State University. She taught psychology at Clark College, Atlanta University, and LeMoyne Junior College in Memphis, Tennessee. In 1943, she was appointed the first female executive director of the Atlanta Urban League. In a special election in 1965, Hamilton and seven other African Americans were elected to the Georgia legislature. Until then, no African American had served in the IN IJEATll Georgialegislature since Reconstruction. Hamilton served in the Georgia senate un- til 1984.She was a principal architect of the 1973 Atlanta city charter which brought African-Americans onto the Atlanta City Council in proportion to their percentage of the population. After her service in the legislature, she was an advisor to the U. S. Civil Rights Commission. Atlanta's Emory University annually hosts the Grace Towns Hamilton lecture. people.biography: Porter. Born enslaved in Jackson, Mississippi, Henry entered the Civil War as a servant but soon deserted to serve with Union forces aboard a U.S. cruiser. After the war, Henry worked as a porter for the New York Life Insurance Company in Savannah, managed by J. C. Johnson and Livingston Mims. He stayed with the company when it moved to Atlanta in 1877. In his role as a porter, he handled millions of dollars in bank deposits during his thirty-year career. He also served as personal valet to Mims, who was mayor of Atlanta from 1901 to 1903. Henry was one of the organizers of the Georgia Real Estate Loan and Trust Company. He served in the Georgia volunteer infantry and was involved in various civic and community organizations. Before moving into the family mansion designed by his mother, Adrienne McNeil Herndon, he lived part of his childhood in the Bumstead Cottage on the campus of Atlanta University. The two-story home had been built by the University's second president, Horace Bumstead. Previously, the Herndons had lived in the boarding house belonging to Francis Norris. Norris Herndon was a graduate of Atlanta University and the business school of Harvard University. As Alonzo Herndon's only heir, he was groomed to manage the family business and fulfill civic and social obligations. In 1905, while still a child, he accompanied his father to the organizing meeting of the Niagara Movement, an early civil rights group. Herndon family biographer Carole Merritt has noted the younger Hemdon's struggles with identity and sexuality. He grew up to be a quiet, reclusive man. He managed Atlanta Lifewith conservative, yet successful strategies, that grew the company into one of the largest African American businesses in the nation. She was chair of the department of foreign languages at North Carolina Central University for almost twenty years. In 1933, she married Rev. Maynard Jackson in Toulouse, and the two spent their honeymoon on the French Riviera. She became a widow in 1953. Jackson was the first African American to receive a library card from the main branch of the Atlanta Public Library (APL). In March 1959, Howard Zinn, a history professor at Spelman, and Whitney Young, dean of Atlanta University's school of social work, started a federal lawsuit against APL with two plaintiffs, Jackson and Rev. Otis Moss, a Morehouse theology student. However, the APL board agreed to desegregate without a court battle, and Jackson applied and received a library card. Earl A. Sanders, professor of music at Spelman, received his card at the same time. According to Jackson's daughter Constance, they received threatening phone calls and were harassed by "drive-by incidents" over the next few days. people.biography: Journalist, Actor, Cinematographer. Jones, an investigativejournalist, was also an actor and producer for radio, film, and stage. He preferred to work as a freelancer, and his articles appeared in the Atlanta Daily World, Chicago Defender, Pittsburgh Courier, and Afro-American newspapers. He was well known for his positive depictions of African American life and culture. His newsreel, "Atlanta's Parade of Progress," was shown across the nation in the early 1940s. Admired for his mellow speaking voice, in the 1930s, Jones' dramatic readings were featured on two NBC radio programs, "WelcomeValley,"where he was the only African American in a cast of thirty-six, and "Life of Uncle Ned," a portrayal of African American life. Jones also produced and hosted his own popular radio show, "Songs of the Southland," featuring the Swanee River Quartette. His broadcast aired on Atlanta's WGST radio station and included poetry, song, and "homely" philosophy. Richardson earned a reputation as a courageous photo journalist. As a member of the Citizens' Defense Committee, he photographed evidence of brutality and civil rights violations. Among the many Georgia cases Jones investigated were the 1946 Moore's Ford lynchings in Monroe, the killing of Henry Gilbert near LaGrange, and the 1948 death penalty sentence given by an all-white American jury in Ellavillefor Rosa Lee Ingram and her teenaged sons, Wallace and Samuel. lllO<JRAPHll'AL L>ICTIONAln' Jones, Mary Agnes Boswell

people.biography: Caterer. Jordan owned and operated her self-named catering business on Howell Mill Road in an affluent white American area of Atlanta. She originally catered from her home with only a friend to assist her, but by the 1970s, Mary Jordan's Catering Service employed more than thirty staffers, including a bridal consultant. Jordan estimated that nearly ninety-nine percent of her clients were white Americans, and many were third generation customers. Though she hired experienced cooks and servers, Jordan trained all her employees in the art of preparing food her way. In 1972, Jordan received a national Pacesetter award from the national Office of Minority Business Enterprise. In addition to her catering business, Jordan was the proprietor of Lake Jordan, a family recreational area that offered boating, fishing, picnicking, and golf for African Americans. One of her sons, Windsor Jordan, worked in the catering business, first as manager, then as CEO.Another son, Vernon Jordan, was executive director of the National Urban League. people.biography: Educator, Minister. Lewis served as both the sixth and eighth president of Morris Brown College.He began his teaching career at Payne Institute in Cuthbert, Georgia, before leaving to attend Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut. He completed a bachelor of divinity degree at Yale in 1913 and a master's degree from the University of Chicago in 1914. He taught at Morris Brown beginning in 1915 and served his first term as president from 1920 to 1928. He was ordained as a minister of the AME Church and pastored Trinity Church in Atlanta. Lewis resigned from Morris Brown following the college's financial decline and declaration of bankruptcy. He relocated to Little Rock, Arkansas, where he served as principal of Dunbar High School and president of Shorter College. people.biography: Librarian. McPheeters was the first professionally trained African American librarian to work in the Atlanta Public Library system. She earned a bachelor's degree in library science from Hampton Institute in Virginia and a master's degree in library science from Columbia Uni- versity in New York. McPheeters worked as a public librarian in Greenville, South Carolina, before being hired in 1934 as assistant librarian at the Auburn Branch of the Atlanta Public Library. Two years later, she was promoted to branch manager. In 1949, she moved to the West Hunter Branch as manager. people.biography: Business Owner, Postmaster. Price, a graduate of the business department of Clark College,operated a general store at the inter- section of Jonesboro and McDonough roads. In 1889, Price was appointed the postmaster for the South Atlanta substation, a branch of the U. S. Post Office that he operated inside his store. He was the first and only African American postmaster in Atlanta at that time. The appointment of African American postmasters across Georgia and the South had resulted in numerous cases of bitter opposition and sometimes violence on the part of white Americans. Price's store was located in the predominantly African American community of Brownsville near Clark College's campus, and his initial appointment apparently did not cause much, if any, contro- versy. The Price family lived above the store until they moved into the new home that Price built on Gammon Avenue in South Atlanta. Price was serving as postmaster for South Atlanta in September 1906 when white Americans rioted in the streets of Atlanta attacking and killing African American cit- izens. Price was arrested and charged with supplying weapons to African American men to defend themselves from the white American rioters. If he had been found guilty, he would have lost his position as postmaster. The case against Price was dis- missed, but he chose to remain in jail for several days for his own safety. An Atlanta school was named in his memory. Price married Minnie Wright

people.biography: Minister. Proctor was the first African American pastor of First Congregational Church. Organized in 1867, the church held services in Storrs Chapel which was located on the corner of Calhoun and Houston Streets. Initially, the congregation was racially integrated, but by 1877, the church was cate- gorized in the Atlanta Constitution as "colored." Proctor began his ministry at the church in 1894. He was a graduate of Fisk University and Yale DivinitySchool. Under his leadership, the church began to emphasize neighborhood outreach and commu- nity service. The congregation established a lending library, a kindergarten, job uaining, an employment bureau, classes for the blind, a home for young working • women, a gymnasium, and a public water fountain. Proctor organized Atlanta's first "Colored Music Festival." The festival series fea- tured artists like Harry Burleigh, an African American classical composer and baritone soloist. When the First Congregational church laid the cornerstone for a new building in 1908, Booker T. Washington was the featured speaker on the pro- gram; George Washington C.arver spoke during the building dedication services in 1909. The First Congregational Church is a Georgia Historical Marker site and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Redding, Wesley Chapel

In 1870, Redding was elected as an officer for Monroe County for the Macon and Western Railroad, and he served as a delegate to the Democratic State Convention from Monroe. "Colonel" Redding, as he was called, was one of the organizers and president of the Atlanta Loan and Trust company, a real estate investment firm. Russell was friends with many local and national business and political leaders, including Martin Luther King Jr. During the height of the Civil Rights Movement, Russell financed bail bonds for jailed activists, and he was a major donor to the Southern Christian Leadership Con- ference. Having saved money from her social security checks for her grandchildren's education, she provided the financial support for Leeto attend Morehouse College.She continued to support her grandson through his graduate studies at New York University's Tisch School of the Arts and provided the seed money for his first feature film, She's Gotta Have It. He later fought to a draw for the middleweight crown against title holder Sam McVey. The fight proved to be one of his most famous. Simmons died at Grady Hospital from a knife wound to the chest. He served as president of the National Insurance Association which recognized him with a distin- guished service award. After retirement, he was elected chair of the board of directors of Atlanta Life. He also served as chairman of the board of Southern Aid/Life of Virginia, a subsidiary of Atlanta Life. Simon was regarded as a pioneer in interracial cooperation and was an active member of the Kiwanis Club and the Conference of Christians and Jews. Simon, Marguerite

She had no formal training in physical education in- struction when she was hired in 1943, but she earned a master's degree in physical education in 1960 from the University of Colorado. Due to her influence and support, the physical education department was established at Spelman, and the college's first fitness and recreation center was built in 1950. Spivey, Mary Robinson

In those early years, the eight men used the Butler Street YMCAas their precinct. They were not allowed to wear their uniforms to and I. from work, and they only patrolled African American sections of the city, on foot. people.biography: Banker, Financial Consultant. Sutton began his career as a bookkeeper for Citizens Trust Bank and rose to the position of executive vice president. He helped many African Americans buy their first homes. Sutton founded a financial consulting business, R. 0. Sutton and Associates. He also served as vice president of finance for Paschal's Concession, Inc. at the Atlanta airport. Sutton was a board member of many business and community organizations, includ- ing the Atlanta Life Insurance Company, the Butler Street YMCA, and the George Washington Carver Boys and Girls Club. people.biography: Restaurant Owner. "Ma" Sutton owned and operated her restaurant on Auburn Avenue for more than thirty years. The name "Ma"was given to her by WWI soldiers who frequented her establishment. When Sutton first arrived in Atlanta from Washington, Georgia, she could neither read nor write, but she learned the alphabet by using the Atlanta Weekly Constitution 1ewspaper.She continued to improve her literacy skills as she gained knowledge and ~rience in business. At her nationally famous restaurant, Sutton took great pride in serving large portions of good food, and she cultivated a comfortable, yet "classy," atmosphere. "Ma Sutton's" was praised as one of the most outstanding African American restaurants in the South. Taylor, Rheubin Marcellus

people.biography: Educator, Civil Rights Leader. Taylor was a high school science and math teacher in the Atlanta Public Schools. He served as president of the Georgia Teachers and Education Association. He and the Atlanta NAACP sued the board of education to grant equal pay for African American teach- ers. NAACP lawyer Constance Baker Motley represented the plaintiffs. Motley was later appointed a federal judge in New York. In 1948, a federal court ordered Georgia public schools to equalize teacher pay. Taylor was fired from the Atlanta Public nroctuPIIH'Al. He appealed to the school board a nd his firing was overturned, however, he was reassigned to an elementary school, a he resigned shortly afterwards. Taylor worked as a conciliations supervisor for e th U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission for seventeen years. He was also a real estate broker and property manager. Thomas, Roscoe Edwin Jr.

people.biography: Lawyer. An alumnus of Morehouse College, Thomas graduated from the University of Michigan Law School in 1947. With only a few years of experience, in 1953, he served as lead counsel for the plaintiffs in Holmes v. Atlanta, the first desegregation lawsuit to be tried in the city. A group of young African American men were denied the right to play at the Bobby Jones Golf Course, a city-owned course. The case eventually reached the U. S. Supreme Court and resulted in the desegregation of all municipal golf courses in Atlanta. Thomas was a founding member of the Gate City Bar Association and served as its third president. He became a specialist in real estate and probate law. He served as general counsel for Citizens Trust Bank, Atlanta Life Insurance Company, and Mutual Federal Savings and Loan. He was a member of the NAACPand the Urban League. Thomas, William Charles

He was widely published as a scholarly writer and in great demand as a national speaker and consultant. Tillman graduated from Morehouse College and received master's and doctoral degrees from the University of Wisconsin. He held various positions at Morehouse and Atlanta University, including professor of English and chairman of the English department at both schools. Tillman also served as dean of the school of arts and sciences at Atlanta University. Earlier on the same day that he died, the trustees of Atlanta University held an award ceremony to recognize his twenty-five years of service to the university. A graduate of Atlanta University, he worked his way through school as a bellhop at the Piedmont hotel during the school year and as a Pullman Porter during his summer breaks. Before joining Atlanta Life as a traveling auditor, Toomer worked as an embalmer for funeral homes in North Carolina and Georgia. During his career at Atlanta Life, he was promoted to chief auditor and ultimately to third vice-president. He also served on the board of directors. He was affiliated with the United Negro College Fund and the YMCA He servedas president of the Lincoln Country Cub. An Atlanta public school was named in his honor. He married Juanita Paschal

people.biography: Mortuary Owner. Trimble began his career in the funeral industry at age twelve sweeping the floors of Hanley's Bell Street Funeral Home. He opened his own mortuary in 1983. At the height of Trimble's career, his mortuary handled an average of eight hundred funerals per year. Trimble was known for his meticulous attention to detail in funeral arrangements and also for the lavish entertainments he held in his home. Trimble staged his final party at his house in Decatur,Georgia-he had left specific instructions regarding his wake. His body, clothedin a red silk embroidered dressing gown, was to be laid out for viewing in his BIOGRAPIIICAL DICTIONARY 245 bedroom, his eye glasses and bible arranged beside him on ivory satin sheets. Thou- sands came to view Trimble's body, and thousands more attended his funeral. Turner, Henry McN eal

people.biography: Educator. Originally named "Basil" for the herb her mother loved to use as a seasoning, Usher changed her name to the more feminine "Bawline" when she entered Atlanta University. Usher began her career at 'the AmericanMissionaryAssociation high school in Virginia. She returned to Atlanta to teach then began moving into administrative positions-elementary school prin- cipal at WesleyAvenue, vice principal at Booker T. Washington High, principal at Howard Junior High. She also completed a master's degree at Atlanta University. In 1951, she was appointed director of instruction for African American students in Atlanta schools-she was the only African American at the time to have an office in City Hall. She was responsible for opening seven new elementary schools during her tenure. In 1943, Usher organized the first African American Girl Scout troop in Atlanta. She was also an avid sports fan and tennis player, and for two years she was the city's AfricanAmerican female tennis champion. A public school was named in her honor, and in 2014 she was designated a Georgia Woman of Achievement. Wallace, Edward B.

He worked his way through Clark College in Atlanta, then Meharry Medical College in Nashville, Tennes- see. After completing his medical degree, Wallace opened a practice in Atlanta, and a drugstore, the Junction Pharmacy. He also served as secretary of the Atlanta Medical Association. After his 1974 retirement from a career in the U.S. Postal Service, Wallace served as Senate Door- keeper in the Georgia Legislature for eighteen sessions. He earned a bachelor of philosophy degree in 1904 from Brown Univer- sity. He was mentored by fellow Brown University graduate John Hope, the first African American president of Morehouse College. Watson served as professor of mathematics and science at Morehouse from 1904 to 1908. After leaving Morehouse, he served as secretary of the Colored Men's Department of the International Com- mittee of the YMCA Watson Memorial Library on the University of Arkansas campus at Pine Bluff was named in his memory. people.biography: Educator, Concert Promoter. During the height of the Great Depression in 1937, Watts used her own funds to bring contralto Marian Anderson to Detroit, Michigan, for her first performance in that city. For twenty- five years, the Nellie Watts Concert Series was an annual tradition in Detroit. It featured artists such as Anderson, Leontyne Price, and Paul Robeson. Robeson, who insisted on being presented by her, dubbed Watts "a fine impresario." The Alvin Ailey Dance Theatre also performed in Watts' concert series. Watts founded the Patron of the Arts organization in Detroit to provide funding for the series and to encourage aspiring performers. Watts was a graduate of Atlanta University and Detroit Teacher's College. She was a teacher in the Detroit public schools, an active clubwoman, and a board member of the Detroit NAACP.She was the daughter of South-View founder Albert Watts. Weatherspool, William Wright

Weatherspool was a gradu- ate of Florida A & M College.He also attended Walker Baptist Institute in Augusta, Georgia, and Moody Bible Institute and the American Bible School, both in Chicago, Illinois. He waspastor of Mount Olive Baptist Church in Atlanta for forty-five years. Mount Olive was in debt $35,000 when he arrived as pastor; the church was worth a million dollars by the time of his retirement. Weatherspool Hall at Mount Olive was named in his honor. Weatherspool was a member of the Atlanta Political and CivicLeague,a leader in the Atlanta Negro Voters League, and co-chair of the Atlanta Bi-Partisan Voters League. Weatherspool died just five weeks after celebrating his 100 th birthday. He married Lillie Sirmans

BIOGRAPII ICAL DI 'TIONARY 249 Westmoreland, Walter Drake (cl 1944) Tuskegee Ainnan. First Lieutenant Water D. Westmoreland graduated from Morehouse Collegeand received his mas- ter's degree from Atlanta University. He earned his pilot wings at the Moton Field flight facility in Tuskegee,Alabama.As a TuskegeeAirmen, he was one of the African American pilots who served in combat with the Army air forces during WWII.West- moreland flew with the 332 00 fighter squadron of the 302 nd Group, Allied Air Command stationed in Italy. Each fighter group painted the tails of their aircraft to uniquely identify them. The members of the 332nd used solid red, hence their nick- name, the "Red Tails." Westmoreland's plane was shot down while providing air support for the beach landing at the port of Anzio in Italy. When he bailed from the disabled aircraft, he broke his leg in two places. After recuperating in a field hospital, he chose to continue flying. His plane was again shot down on October 13, 1944, while returning from an escort mission to Blechammer, Germany. Westmoreland was killed; his body was ultimately recoveredand returned to Atlanta in 1949. Westmoreland was the son of William G. Westmorela

people.biography: Educator, Author. Whiting was a grad- uate of Howard University, in Washington, D. C. and taught at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. Considered a pioneer in progressive elementary education, she was ap- pointed coordinator for the Jeanes teachers program in Georgia. Whiting also held various other positions in Georgia education-she was principal of the elementary department of the laboratory school at Atlanta University, State Supervisor of Afri- can American elementary schools, and coordinator of student teaching at the GeorgiaDepartment of Education. Whiting served on several national educational committees, including President Herbert Hoover's White House Conference on Child Health and Protection, the Committee on Elementary Education, and the Na- tional Conference on the Fundamental Problems in Negro Education. Whiting published two books for children that emphasized African American history and heritage: Negro Folk Tales for Children of Primary Grades and Negro Art, Music, Rhyme, and Dance for Young Folks. people.biography: Minister,Poet.Whitman was bom eMlaved in Kentucky. After the end of the Civil War, he worked in manual labor jobs. He was primarily self-taught, however, with only a few months of schooling he began to teach. He entered Wilberforce University but only stayed for six months. It was at Wilberforce that he met the school's president, Bishop Daniel Alexander Payne of the AME Church. Whitman became Bishop Payne's protege. He founded and pastored churches in Ohio, Kansas, Texas, and Georgia, and be served as the general financial agent at Wilberforce. In Atlanta, Whitman pastored Allen Temple. While following the ministry, Whitman also found time to write. He was the first African American to publish a poem in Spenserian stall1.3,"Twasinta's Seminoles." He also composed one of the longest poems ever written by an African American, "Not a Man and Yet a Man." Whitman struggled with alcoholism throughout his life, and his addiction may have hampered both his ministerial and writing career. He married Caddie (aka Katie) Whibnan

people.biography: . She was a skilled orator and the president of the Women's Council of the Nineteenth Century. The organiza- tion, which Caddie Whitman founded, encouraged African American women's participation in the moral growth and future of the race. In 1893, on "Colored Amer- icans' Day"at Chicago'sWorld Columbian Exhibition, she read her husband's poem, "Freedom's Triumphant Song," a composition be wrote for the occasion. They were parents of "The Whitman Sisters," a traveling vaudeville act. Caddie Whitman was not only her daughters' chaperone on the road but also their first business manager-unusual in a time when white American men generally managed Afri- can American performers on the vaudeville circuit. people.biography: were part of a vaudeville touring act in the early part of the twentieth century. They were the daugh- ters of Albery Alison and Caddie Whitman. The sisters began singing, dancing, and playing guitar in their father's church and later, Mabel and Essie, billed as "The Danzette Sisters," toured throughout the South and in Europe. Alberta joined the group and the sisters continued to tour on both the white and African American vaud(.,>ville circuits. The sisters were light skinned enough to pass for white and sometimes wore blackface makeup while performing. In 1904, they made news by demanding that the Jefferson theater in Birmingham, Alabama, integrate seating on the main floor. Mabel was the eldest sister and followed her mother as the group's manager. Essiehad a distinct contralto voice and was a quick-witted comedian. She designed and made the group's costumes. Essie became a preacher in Chicago after her retire- mentfrom show business, and the sisters bought a home together in the city. Alberta, calledBert, was a flash dancer and a celebrated male impersonator. She handled the musicand composed much of the group's material. Performing as the "Whitman Sisters Revue," the company grew to more than forty performers, including Eddie "Rochester" Anderson, Count Basie, and Moms Mahley.Twelve-year-old tap dancer Bill "Bojangles" Robinson got his start with the Whitman sisters. people.biography: Domestic Servant. Williams, born during slavery, was the namesake for a popular Smyrna, Georgia, restaurant called "Aunt Fanny's Cabin." The restaurant was owned by a member of the white American Campbell family that Williams had worked for during slavery and in freedom. Images of Williams, dressed in a white head kerchief and apron, were featured in the restau- rant's advertising. Williams was active in her community and at the Wheat Street Baptist Church. She received an award for being the top fund raiser in a campaign to build a hospital for African Americans in Marietta. Williams, Samuel Woodrow

people.biography: Minister, Educator, Civil Rights Leader. A native of Arkansas, Williams earned undergraduate degrees at Morehouse College and Howard University. He continued his studies at Howard to earn a master's degree, and he completed doctoral degrees at the University of Chicago and Arkansas Baptist College. In Atlanta, Williams was pastor of Friendship Baptist Church from 1954 until his death. He also served as chairman and professor in the philosophy and religion department at Morehouse College. Active in civic affairs, Williams was president of the Atlanta Branch of the NAACP and a member of the executive committee. In 1959, he was one of the plaintiffs in a successful Atlanta city bus desegregation lawsuit. He held various leadership positions in the SCLC, the Atlanta Summit Leadership Conference, the Greater Atlanta Council on Human Relations, and the Georgia Council on Human Relations. His widow, Billye Williams, married major league baseball player Hank Aaron. Williamson, Quentin V. Sr.

people.biography: Blues Singer. In 1940s Atlanta, Wright was called the "Prince of the Blues." He had a high-pitched vocal range, wore his hair styled in a pompadour, and dressed elaborately for the stage. All of which "Little Richard" Penniman acknowledged he copied from Wright, the man he called his idol. Wright was born in Atlanta and began singing gospel music as a child at Mount Vernon Baptist Church. Wright was not only a popular entertainer in Atlanta, he also performed at venues such as the Apollo Theater in New York City and the Howard Theater in Washington, D. C. Wright began recording with Savoy records in 1949 and released a number of top ten records, including "Blues for My Baby," "Stacked Deck," and "Hey Little Girl." Wynn, Ida Elizabeth Landrum

people.biography: . Arthur Yancey was a mail carrier and served as president of the Atlanta Letter Carriers Association, a professional organization for African American postal workers. After Arthur Yancey's retirement, in 1959, he wrote a book, lnterposition- ulification: What the Negro May Expect, an autobiographical account of his life in rural Georgia told in sketches, stories, and poems. Arthur Yancey was also a frequent contributor to the Atlanta Daily World through his letters to the editor. In 1920, Arthur Yancey, his wife, and their infant son Orlando traveled to Brazil where Yancey planned to start an export business. While in Brazil, he was attracted to Catholicismand the work the church was doing among the Brazilian people. When he returned to Atlanta, he converted to Catholicism and began his work in the CatholicChurch. In 1960 at his parish, St. Paul of the Cross, Yancey was recognized by the Pope for his faith and devotion and was given the medal Pro Ecclesia et Pon- tifice,one of the highest awards of the Vatican. Daisy Yancey attended Atlanta public schools and the Atlanta University Normal School. She was elected president of the Neighborhood Union in 1950 and served until the organization officially disbanded in 1962. Asa Yancey graduated from Morehouse College and the University of Michigan Medical School. He studied under Dr. Charles R. Drew at Freedmen's Hospital at the Howard University School of Medicine in Washington D. C. He served as chief of surgery at Tuskegee Veterans Hospital for ten years before joining the faculty at Emory. He was chief of surgery at Hughe

people.biography: Business Owner. Yates, a graduate of More- house College, was co-owner and chief operating officer of the Yates and Milton Drugstore chain. He served as board chair of Citizens Trust Bank. He also served as president of the South-View Cemetery Association. He was the first African Ameri- can named to the Fulton-DeKalb County Hospital Authority. Yates served as vice president of both the Southeastern Fire Insurance Company and Mutual Federal Savings and Loan. He married Mae Maxwell

people.biography: Social Worker. She succeeded her mother, Clara M. Pitts, as director of the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home (CSPH). At the time of Yates' appointment in 1950, CSPH was still the only fulltime child care agency in Atlanta for African American children. Under her direction, the home continued to expand and modernize its facilities, and in 1964 she relocated CSPH to Fairburn Road. The new location featured cottage-style residences for the children plus room for future expansion. She served on the faculty of Atlanta University's School of Social Work and was a charter member of the National Association of Social Workers. She was the first recipient of the Atlanta Urban League's Jesse O. Thomas Community Service Award. Yates, Ella Gaines

A Morehouse graduate, Williamson owned one of the large t :-J N DEATll and the sisters continued to tour on both the white and African American vaud(.,>ville circuits. The sisters were light skinned enough to pass for white and sometimes wore blackface makeup while performing. In 1904, they made news by demanding that the Jefferson theater in Birmingham, Alabama, integrate seating on the main floor. Mabel was the eldest sister and followed her mother as the group's manager. Essiehad a distinct contralto voice and was a quick-witted comedian. She designed and made the group's costumes. Essie became a preacher in Chicago after her retire- mentfrom show business, and the sisters bought a home together in the city. Alberta, calledBert, was a flash dancer and a celebrated male impersonator. She handled the musicand composed much of the group's material. Performing as the "Whitman Sisters Revue," the company grew to more than forty performers, including Eddie "Rochester" Anderson, Count Basie, and Moms Mahley.Twelve-year-old tap dancer Bill "Bojangles" Robinson got his start with the Whitman sisters. people.biography: Minister,Poet.Whitman was bom eMlaved in Kentucky. After the end of the Civil War, he worked in manual labor jobs. He was primarily self-taught, however, with only a few months of schooling he began to teach. He entered Wilberforce University but only stayed for six months. It was at Wilberforce that he met the school's president, Bishop Daniel Alexander Payne of the AME Church. Whitman became Bishop Payne's protege. He founded and pastored churches in Ohio, Kansas, Texas, and Georgia, and be served as the general financial agent at Wilberforce. In Atlanta, Whitman pastored Allen Temple. While following the ministry, Whitman also found time to write. He was the first African American to publish a poem in Spenserian stall1.3,"Twasinta's Seminoles." He also composed one of the longest poems ever written by an African American, "Not a Man and Yet a Man." Whitman struggled with alcoholism throughout his life, and his addiction may have hampered both his ministerial and writing career. He married Caddie (aka Katie) Whibnan

people.biography: . She was a skilled orator and the president of the Women's Council of the Nineteenth Century. The organiza- tion, which Caddie Whitman founded, encouraged African American women's participation in the moral growth and future of the race. In 1893, on "Colored Amer- icans' Day"at Chicago'sWorld Columbian Exhibition, she read her husband's poem, "Freedom's Triumphant Song," a composition be wrote for the occasion. They were parents of "The Whitman Sisters," a traveling vaudeville act. Caddie Whitman was not only her daughters' chaperone on the road but also their first business manager-unusual in a time when white American men generally managed Afri- can American performers on the vaudeville circuit. people.biography: Educator, Author. Whiting was a grad- uate of Howard University, in Washington, D. C. and taught at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. Considered a pioneer in progressive elementary education, she was ap- pointed coordinator for the Jeanes teachers program in Georgia. Whiting also held various other positions in Georgia education-she was principal of the elementary department of the laboratory school at Atlanta University, State Supervisor of Afri- can American elementary schools, and coordinator of student teaching at the GeorgiaDepartment of Education. Whiting served on several national educational committees, including President Herbert Hoover's White House Conference on Child Health and Protection, the Committee on Elementary Education, and the Na- tional Conference on the Fundamental Problems in Negro Education. Whiting published two books for children that emphasized African American history and heritage: Negro Folk Tales for Children of Primary Grades and Negro Art, Music, Rhyme, and Dance for Young Folks. A school in Tucker, Georgia, was named in her honor. She married Joseph L. Whiting

people.biography: Educator. Whiting served as director of education at Tuskegee before being appointed as a YMCA secretary in Montoir, France, during WWI. BIOCl<APlll('AI. DICTION RY 2/,t Westmoreland, Walter Drake (cl 1944) Tuskegee Ainnan. First Lieutenant Water D. Westmoreland graduated from Morehouse Collegeand received his mas- ter's degree from Atlanta University. He earned his pilot wings at the Moton Field flight facility in Tuskegee,Alabama.As a TuskegeeAirmen, he was one of the African American pilots who served in combat with the Army air forces during WWII.West- moreland flew with the 332 00 fighter squadron of the 302 nd Group, Allied Air Command stationed in Italy. Each fighter group painted the tails of their aircraft to uniquely identify them. The members of the 332nd used solid red, hence their nick- name, the "Red Tails." Westmoreland's plane was shot down while providing air support for the beach landing at the port of Anzio in Italy. When he bailed from the disabled aircraft, he broke his leg in two places. After recuperating in a field hospital, he chose to continue flying. His plane was again shot down on October 13, 1944, while returning from an escort mission to Blechammer, Germany. Westmoreland was killed; his body was ultimately recoveredand returned to Atlanta in 1949. Westmoreland was the son of William G. Westmoreland

people.biography: Educator, Concert Promoter. During the height of the Great Depression in 1937, Watts used her own funds to bring contralto Marian Anderson to Detroit, Michigan, for her first performance in that city. For twenty- five years, the Nellie Watts Concert Series was an annual tradition in Detroit. It featured artists such as Anderson, Leontyne Price, and Paul Robeson. Robeson, who insisted on being presented by her, dubbed Watts "a fine impresario." The Alvin Ailey Dance Theatre also performed in Watts' concert series. Watts founded the Patron of the Arts organization in Detroit to provide funding for the series and to encourage aspiring performers. Watts was a graduate of Atlanta University and Detroit Teacher's College. She was a teacher in the Detroit public schools, an active clubwoman, and a board member of the Detroit NAACP.She was the daughter of South-View founder Albert Watts. Weatherspool, William Wright

people.biography: Minister. Weatherspool was a gradu- ate of Florida A & M College.He also attended Walker Baptist Institute in Augusta, Georgia, and Moody Bible Institute and the American Bible School, both in Chicago, Illinois. He waspastor of Mount Olive Baptist Church in Atlanta for forty-five years. Mount Olive was in debt $35,000 when he arrived as pastor; the church was worth a million dollars by the time of his retirement. Weatherspool Hall at Mount Olive was named in his honor. Weatherspool was a member of the Atlanta Political and CivicLeague,a leader in the Atlanta Negro Voters League, and co-chair of the Atlanta Bi-Partisan Voters League. Weatherspool died just five weeks after celebrating his 100 th birthday. He married Lillie Sirmans

people.biography: , son of Edward and Birdie, was one of the first African Americans to join the marines. After his 1974 retirement from a career in the U.S. Postal Service, Wallace served as Senate Door- keeper in the Georgia Legislature for eighteen sessions. Watson served as professor of mathematics and science at Morehouse from 1904 to 1908. After leaving Morehouse, he served as secretary of the Colored Men's Department of the International Com- mittee of the YMCA Watson Memorial Library on the University of Arkansas campus at Pine Bluff was named in his memory. She returned to Atlanta to teach then began moving into administrative positions-elementary school prin- cipal at WesleyAvenue, vice principal at Booker T. Washington High, principal at Howard Junior High. She also completed a master's degree at Atlanta University. In 1951, she was appointed director of instruction for African American students in Atlanta schools-she was the only African American at the time to have an office in City Hall. She was responsible for opening seven new elementary schools during her tenure. In 1943, Usher organized the first African American Girl Scout troop in Atlanta. She was also an avid sports fan and tennis player, and for two years she was the city's AfricanAmerican female tennis champion. A public school was named in her honor, and in 2014 she was designated a Georgia Woman of Achievement. Wallace, Edward B.

people.biography: Lawyer. An alumnus of Morehouse College, Thomas graduated from the University of Michigan Law School in 1947. With only a few years of experience, in 1953, he served as lead counsel for the plaintiffs in Holmes v. Atlanta, the first desegregation lawsuit to be tried in the city. A group of young African American men were denied the right to play at the Bobby Jones Golf Course, a city-owned course. The case eventually reached the U. S. Supreme Court and resulted in the desegregation of all municipal golf courses in Atlanta. Thomas was a founding member of the Gate City Bar Association and served as its third president. people.biography: Shoemaker, Entrepreneur. Schell arrived in Atlanta in 1876 with a total savings of $3.75. That first night in Atlanta, he had no place to sleep, but he soon found work with A. J. Delbridge, an African American shoemaker. After several more years of working and saving his earnings, Schell opened his own shoe shop. people.biography: Minister. Proctor was the first African American pastor of First Congregational Church. Organized in 1867, the church held services in Storrs Chapel which was located on the corner of Calhoun and Houston Streets. Initially, the congregation was racially integrated, but by 1877, the church was cate- gorized in the Atlanta Constitution as "colored." Proctor began his ministry at the church in 1894. He was a graduate of Fisk University and Yale DivinitySchool. Under his leadership, the church began to emphasize neighborhood outreach and commu- nity service. The congregation established a lending library, a kindergarten, job uaining, an employment bureau, classes for the blind, a home for young working • women, a gymnasium, and a public water fountain. Proctor organized Atlanta's first "Colored Music Festival." The festival series fea- tured artists like Harry Burleigh, an African American classical composer and baritone soloist. When the First Congregational church laid the cornerstone for a new building in 1908, Booker T. Washington was the featured speaker on the pro- gram; George Washington C.arver spoke during the building dedication services in 1909. people.biography: Business Owner, Postmaster. Price, a graduate of the business department of Clark College,operated a general store at the inter- section of Jonesboro and McDonough roads. In 1889, Price was appointed the postmaster for the South Atlanta substation, a branch of the U. S. Post Office that he operated inside his store. He was the first and only African American postmaster in Atlanta at that time. The appointment of African American postmasters across Georgia and the South had resulted in numerous cases of bitter opposition and sometimes violence on the part of white Americans. Price's store was located in the predominantly African American community of Brownsville near Clark College's campus, and his initial appointment apparently did not cause much, if any, contro- versy. The Price family lived above the store until they moved into the new home that Price built on Gammon Avenue in South Atlanta. Price was serving as postmaster for South Atlanta in September 1906 when white Americans rioted in the streets of Atlanta attacking and killing African American cit- izens. Price was arrested and charged with supplying weapons to African American men to defend themselves from the white American rioters. If he had been found guilty, he would have lost his position as postmaster. The case against Price was dis- missed, but he chose to remain in jail for several days for his own safety. An Atlanta school was named in his memory. Price married Minnie Wright

She earned a bachelor's degree in library science from Hampton Institute in Virginia and a master's degree in library science from Columbia Uni- versity in New York. McPheeters worked as a public librarian in Greenville, South Carolina, before being hired in 1934 as assistant librarian at the Auburn Branch of the Atlanta Public Library. Two years later, she was promoted to branch manager. In 1949, she moved to the West Hunter Branch as manager. McPheeters achieved another "first" in 1966 when she became the first African American reference librarian at Georgia State University. The West Hunter Branch Library was renamed in her honor as the Washington Park/ Annie L. McPheeters Branch Library. people.biography: Sexton. "Brother" Matthews was the sexton of Big Bethel AME Church for more than fifty years. people.biography: Caterer. Jordan owned and operated her self-named catering business on Howell Mill Road in an affluent white American area of Atlanta. She originally catered from her home with only a friend to assist her, but by the 1970s, Mary Jordan's Catering Service employed more than thirty staffers, including a bridal consultant. Jordan estimated that nearly ninety-nine percent of her clients were white Americans, and many were third generation customers. Though she hired experienced cooks and servers, Jordan trained all her employees in the art of preparing food her way. people.biography: Insurance Executive, Philanthropist. Herndon succeeded his father, Alonzo F. Herndon, as president of Atlanta Life Insurance Company. Before moving into the family mansion designed by his mother, Adrienne McNeil Herndon, he lived part of his childhood in the Bumstead Cottage on the campus of Atlanta University. The two-story home had been built by the University's second president, Horace Bumstead. Previously, the Herndons had lived in the boarding house belonging to Francis Norris. Norris Herndon was a graduate of Atlanta University and the business school of Harvard University. As Alonzo Herndon's only heir, he was groomed to manage the family business and fulfill civic and social obligations. In 1905, while still a child, he accompanied his father to the organizing meeting of the Niagara Movement, an early civil rights group. Herndon family biographer Carole Merritt has noted the younger Hemdon's struggles with identity and sexuality. He grew up to be a quiet, reclusive man. He managed Atlanta Lifewith conservative, yet successful strategies, that grew the company into one of the largest African American businesses in the nation. Like his father, he was well regarded for his philanthropy to organizations such as the United Negro College Fund, the NMCP, and the National Urban League. IN DEATH Henderson, Rogers

people.biography: Carpenter, Building Contractor. According to Atlanta historian Edward R. Carter, Hamilton served in the Union Army during the CivilWar, was elected to the city council of Eufaula, Alabama, and served two terms in Alabama's Reconstruction Legislature. Hamilton built many fine homes in Eufala, including his own. He was given a gold watch and a piece of property by the city of Eufala for the part he played in preventing a fire and robbery secretly being plotted by African Americans. By 1876, Hamilton had moved his family to Atlanta and started the construction company of Alexander Hamilton and Son. Hamilton's obituary in the Atlanta Constitution on May 27, 1911, noted that "some of the best-known buildings in Atlanta were erected by him." Two of those structures included the Good Samaritan building on Ivy Street and the Linton Hopkins House in Ansley Park. Hamilton also built many of the large houses on Peachtree and Washington streets. He worked as superintendent at W. L. Trainer & Company for several years, and he also was the contractor for Morris Brown College. Hamilton was one of the organizers of the Georgia Real Estate Loan and Trust Company and a member of the National Negro Business League. people.biography: Musician, Educator. Carver was a jazz flutist and pro- fessor of music at Clark College, his alma mater. He gained his first professional experience performing with Atlanta band leader J. Neal Montgomery. In the early 193os, Carver recorded with famous band leaders such as Dave Nelson, Spike Hughes, and Benny Carter. Carver also played saxophone and flute with drummer ChickWebb's orchestra. After Webb died, Ella Fitzgerald took over the Webb orches- tra. and Carver continued to play with the group for a time. In 1942, Carver joined the Clark College faculty. He directed the concert and marching bands, and he wrote the music to Clark's fight song, "Hail Roaring Panther." During his undergraduate years at Clark, he organized a band with fellow students called the "Collegiate Ramblers" or sometimes, "The Collegians." Carver earned a master's degree in music education from VanderCook College of Music in Orica.go,Illinois, in 1952. Under the administration of Jessie M. Wartman, music supervisorof Atlanta's elementary schools for African Americans, Carver organized the first elementary school bands. The news of Bushyhead'sburial in an African American cemetery prompted local white Ameri- cans to suggest that funds be raised to move his body to the Confederate section of Oakland, the city cemetery. Andrews was involved in many health and community service organizations-she was an original board member of the Atlanta Urban League, vol- unteered with the Community Chest, served as a board member in the colored branch of the Atlanta Tuberculosis Association, and was a life member of the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA She was a charter member of the Neighborhood Union and served as its second president from 1937 to 1942. people.biography: Pharmacist. Following in the footsteps of his uncle Moses Amos, Georgia's first African American licensed pharmacist, Miles Amos be- came proprietor of the West Side Drug Store upon his uncle's death in 1928. The next year the store began advertising as Amos' Drugstore. Amos worked his way through Wilberforce College in Ohio with a summer job as a Pullman Porter. He graduated from Cincinnati College of Pharmacy in 1928. In 1953, Amos and two other African Americans, Austin Thomas Walden and Roderick Badger Harris, won a court deci- sion to qualify for election to the City Executive Committee, a nonpartisan political organization responsible for conducting Atlanta's primary elections. Amos won over Harris, and Walden ran unopposed. Amos continued to be involved with Atlanta's civic and political affairs throughout his life, and he was a lifetime member of the NAACP.He married his cousin India DeLaine Amos

Carter published Our Pulpit fllustrated: Biographical Sketches of 138 MEMORY IN DEATH CHAPTER 13 Genealogy in the Cemetery Landscape Gravestones represent a unique historical resource for genealogists and family historians. Most gravestone inscriptions have basic biographical information-the name of the deceased and birth and death dates-but some gravestones may also include maiden names, the names of spouses, the location of death and birth, occupations, and military, social, and religious affiliations. For young children, a gravestone inscription may be the only record of their short lives. The name of a spouse on a gravestone may be the only record of a marriage between enslaved African Americans, whose marriages during slavery were not legal and only rarely documented. Spatial relationships in the cemetery-the location and arrangement of grave- stones and burial lots-may offer clues to help identify previously unknown family relationships. Gray (1917)"Sleep on darling, I will meet you again." 124 MEMORY IN DEATH CHAPTER 12 Epitaphs-Gone But Not Forgotten Epitaphs preserve the memory of the dead. They are an invitation to the living to remember those who have passed on. The Latin equivalent, epitaphium (over the tomb), originally referred to a funeral oration-a speech given literally over the grave of the deceased. Later, the term was also used to refer to the specific part of a gravestone inscription that describes the life of the deceased. Gravestone epitaphs preserve the legacy of the departed by documenting their values, beliefs, and life achievements. Some details in the inscription are not considered part of the actual epitaph. These include the dates of death and birth, the place of death, relationships ("Wife of," "Father of," etc.), and other standard text such as "In memory of" and "Erected by." An epitaph can be inscribed on a gravestone, written as an obituary, or read or spoken as part of a funeral ritual. Epitaphs often serve as examples of virtuous living for those left behind. During the Victorian era, the selection of appropriate epitaphs-to commemorate the worth of the individual and to provide comfort to the bereaved-became an important aspect of the memorialization of the dead. Loved ones found comfort in phrases such as "At Rest" and "Rest in Peace," perhaps the simplest and most frequently seen epitaphs of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The tablets varied somewhat in design and construction, but they were typically cast in advance then customized as needed. The markers were fashioned from two parts; the main tablet was formed from concrete aggregate, and a smaller plaster tablet was later attached to its surface. This early design did not have a footing to stabilize it; the vertical marker was sunk into the ground deep enough to hold it upright, and the area around it was filled in with dirt. Over the years as the ground has settled, some of the markers at South-View have sunk even deeper into the earth, others have shifted or tilted, and many have been broken into scattered fragments. However, a number of markers still remain upright or are mostly intact, and these markers provide historical evidence that otherwise might not have survived in any other way. In addition to the name of the funeral home, the plaster tablet was inscribed with the name of the deceased, the date of death, and birth date, if known. How·ever, by the late nineteenth century, more African Americans were adopting the European style burial practices seen in white American cemeteries. Especially in urban cemeteries like South-View,African Americans were erecting elaborate markers featuring Christian or Victoriansymbols-though often crafted in concrete, not stone. The wooden headboards and grave goods are long gone, but South-View'shistoric section retains a large number of concrete grave markers that reflect the continuing prevalence of vernacular memorial traditions in the twentieth century along with the European influence of rural cemetery design. Plain and decorativeconcrete markers were widelyused by families at South-View who could not afford, or perhaps chose not to buy, more expensive stone markers. Concrete markers became popular, in part, because they were inexpensive,but also because they proved more durable than other vernacular forms. The styles of concrete grave markers erected at South- View varied from thin vertical slabs in simple shapes that could be inscribed with a nail or other sharp object, to large, elaborate markers replete with Victorian motifs and symbols. On February 20, 1886, the Atlanta Constitution reported the intent of South-View's owners to make it "the most beautiful colored cemetery in the South." 1 The site for the new cemetery lay along McDonough Road about four miles from downtown. Atlanta's city engineer, Thomas A. Clayton, was asked to submit a bid for surveying and laying off the grounds. 2 Whether Clayton ever submitted a bid, or had a bid accepted, is unknown. South-View's oral history contends that officials of Westview Cemetery aided in the establishment of South-View, but the nature and extent ofWestview's purported involvement is undocumented. However, the burial of Sterling Watts in Westview's Rest Haven may have prompted his son Albert to confront Westview officialsregard- ing the cemetery's conditions for African American burials. South-View's oral history describes the response of Westview officials to such criticism: "If you don't like it, start your own cemetery."3 While the landscape design of Westview followed the newer "lawn" cemetery style, the terracing and walled lots at South-View emulate the older design used at Oakland Cemetery.
